# Copper March 2010 

- The closing stages of March saw the return of risk appetite which resulted in official 3-month quotes hitting $7823/t on the 30th; their highest level since August 2008.  Prior to this, the month was shaping up to be rather directionless with official 3-month prices trading within a narrow range of just $280/t through to the 26th, compared with $1105/t during February. 

- We still remain to be convinced that current prices are reflective of current market fundamentals.  We work from the premise that at normal stock levels (65 days), fundamentally-driven prices (i.e. excluding non-fundamental influences) are fully justified at $4,400/t as opposed to $7700/t.  We are also still of the opinion that the sheer weight of investment fund money flow into commodities that has created the current “multiplier effect” has been exaggerated by the lack of alternative investments (due to lower interest rates, poor profitability from within the non-cyclical equity markets etc). 

- We forecast that global refined copper consumption will increase by 5.4% this year to just above 18.2Mt.  Previously we were forecasting growth of 5.7% to ~18.5Mt.  The lower forecast reflected the knock–on effect of a downward revision we made to our Chinese estimate for last year. 

- As the first quarter of 2010 draws to a close the general lack of spot concentrate business thus far this year can be ascribed to a combination of tight market conditions and to a desire by various buyers and sellers to transact their business in a less overt manner than has previously been the case.  The only spot deals that emerged this month arose from Chilean producers and these appeared to have been sold to the trade in the range LME flat to less than $5/t & 0.5c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Prices lacked direction for the majority of the month** The closing stages of March saw the return of risk appetite which resulted in official 3-month quotes hitting $7823/t on the 30<sup>th</sup> ; their highest level since August 2008.  Prior to this, the month was shaping up to be rather directionless with official 3-month prices trading within a narrow range of just

$280/t through to the 26th, compared with $1105/t during February.  This narrow range masked a fair degree of volatility during the period as evidenced by daily min/max variations in official 3-month quotes from -$198/t and +$264/t.  As a consequence, prices ranged from a peak of $7581/t on the 8<sup>th</sup> to the month’s low of $7301/t on the 15<sup>th</sup> .  Through to the 26<sup>th</sup> the market was supported by fundamental factors, a significant rise in cancelled warrants and by positive economic data from the US.  Meanwhile on the downside, prices came under pressure from declining Chinese buying interest (a reminder of the possibility of the introduction of additional monetary tightening policies) as well as growing concerns about the Greek debt situation given the potential knock-on effect of this on other European economies. 

**Chilean earthquake supports prices** Relative to the end of February the first week of March saw official quotes (3month) increasing from $7096/t to $7581/t (as of the 8<sup>th</sup> ).  The main impetus for the $485/t rally was a major earthquake which hit Chile on Saturday 27<sup>th</sup> February and measured 8.8 in magnitude.  Various mining operations were forced to suspend production over the weekend (see PRODUCTION) which was reflected in official 3m quotes rising by $264/t on the 1<sup>st</sup> to settle at $7335/t.  However, it soon became evident that the impact of the initial earthquake on these Chilean production facilities had been (surprisingly) relatively minor.  Nevertheless, the sheer number of large aftershocks coupled with reports about the fragility of the country’s power grid and transport infrastructure only served to heighten market uncertainty about the ongoing security of raw materials and metals supplies from the world’s largest copper producer.  Last year Chile’s mine production totalled 5.4Mt which accounted for 34% of global output.  This not only provided initial support to prices during the first week of March but it also ensured against there being any move towards a significant sell-off during the remainder of the month. 

**Sharp rise in LME cancelled warrants** Also supporting prices during the first week was a significant rise in LME cancelled warrants.  Warrants marked for delivery out of LME warehouses rose from 26.2kt at the end of February to a peak of 36kt on the 2<sup>nd</sup> .  The majority of the increase reflected an 8.1kt uplift in cancelled warrants located in European warehouses.  This reflected consumers’ concerns about potential delays to their contracted shipments from Chile, forcing them to make alternative supply arrangements.  Also, another price-supportive factor between the 1<sup>st</sup> and the 8<sup>th</sup> was the release of stronger-than-expected US non-farm payrolls data. 

**Bearish sentiment during the second week** Between the 9<sup>th</sup> and the 15<sup>th</sup> market sentiment turned less positive as concerns waned over future supply di

sruptions in Chile. The market’s focus was redirected towards China and the spectre of additional action by the authorities to further tighten monetary policy following the recent release of strong CPI data. According to China’s National Bureau of Statistics the country’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased by 2.7% in February from a year earlier. This followed an annual gain of 1.5% in January. As a consequence, official prices (3m) trended lower, trading down from the month’s high of $7581/t on the 8th to the month’s low of $7301/t on the 15th . **Risk appetite returns** Since the 15th prices have recovered markedly and are currently trading around $7830/t. In recent days official quotes have been supported by a weaker US dollar, following the EU agreement on how to tackle Greece’s debt problem, more large earthquakes in Chile (on the 26th ) and the return of risk appetite. Through to the 30th official prices (3-month) averaged $7478/t. This was up by 8.8% from February’s average of $6871/t. ### **Physical copper spot premia rates ($/t)** 200 W Europe Shanghai 10.0

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - March 2010 Page 2 of 26 Copper Monthly Update **Exchange stocks fall in March** Total exchange stocks fell during the month with net declines in LME and Comex inventories outweighed by a net increase in SHFE stocks. As of the 30th , total inventories were 761.5kt, equivalent to 15.2 days of consumption. This was down by 31.4kt from February’s level of 794.4kt and, perhaps more importantly, represented the first month of decline since June last year. Most of the fall resulted from a 37kt reduction in LME inventories to 514.3kt. European warehouses recorded the largest withdrawals with outflows totalling a net 19.2kt, most notably in Rotterdam where inventories fell by a net 14.9kt to 30.4kt. As noted earlier, the decline in European LME warrants were more to do with concerns over possible late deliveries from Chile than any significant improvement in underlying demand. At the time of writing (the 30th ), LME cancelled warrants totalled 18.6kt. While down from the month’s peak of 35kt on the 2nd , this still suggests that further withdrawals will take place in the coming weeks. Elsewhere, Comex cathode stocks fell by a net 2kt to 91.7kt. Similar to Europe, the decline resulted from concern over future Chilean deliveries rather than from a pick up in demand. Meanwhile in China, SHFE inventories increased for the third consecutive month rising by a net 6kt to 155.5kt. This was their highest level since September 2002 and in part reflected the massive upli

ft in imported scrap receipts (see below) during the first two months of the year. **European premia remain elevated** European premia remained at high levels during the month despite no significant recovery in demand. The main supporting factors were metal tightly held by certain market players and delays in cathode deliveries. We have heard that warrants held by two major market players were responsible for this artificial tightness. With the market in contango it has been possible to finance the cost of holding material away from the visible exchanges. This factor, combined with the delays in cathode shipments continued to lend support to premia with grade A material and Chilean cathodes from Rotterdam commanding a price of $70/t over LME. Although down from $80/t last month this still represented a high level given that there has been no significant recovery in underlying demand. Elsewhere, Italian warrants continued to trade around $75/t while standard grade cathode remained at $20/t over LME due to tight scrap supplies. **US premia supported by tight scrap availability** US premia edged upwards during the month, increasing from 3.54c/lb at the end of February, to 4-4.5c/lb in March. These higher quotes were the result of a shortage of higher grade scrap, rather than any improvement in underlying demand. Our sources have reconfirmed that high grade copper scrap remains in short supply because of the ongoing slowdown in industrial activity last year. This has forced some consumers to purchase cathode as a substitute. Until there is a meaningful pick up in industrial activity we would expect tight scrap conditions to continue supporting US premia in the coming months. **Chinese premia weaken** Chinese premia weakened during March, falling from $110/t at the end of February to $90/t during March. This lower level reflected reduced arbitrage opportunities with SHFE prices trading at a discount to LME quotes throughout the majority of the month. ### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**Chinese refined imports fall in February from a year earlier** According to the latest Chinese trade data refined imports fell by 18.6% year on year in February to 221kt. However, on a month-on-month basis receipts were up by 12% (+24kt) from January. This was not surprising and reflected favourable arbitrage conditions in January with SHFE quotes exceeding LME prices by an average $145/t (exclusive of VAT). Chinese imports of copper scrap increased by 26.7% year on year in February which needs to be viewed in the context of the sharp decline in scrap imports a year e

arlier. For the first two months as a whole, copper scrap imports jumped by 52.5% from the corresponding period in 2009 (Chinese scrap imports last year fell by 28% year on year). However, there is the potential for copper scrap imports to slow following new legislation that is due to be introduced by the China’s General Administration of Customs on April 1st . Metals Market Service Monthly Update - March 2010 Page 3 of 26 Copper Monthly Update This will require copper scrap importers to clearly declare the metal content of their imports. This should help to eliminate the previous practice of understating the copper content of imported scrap in order to reduce the amount of VAT payable (imports of copper scrap and refined metal are subject to 17% VAT). The new legislation should see closer scrutiny of cargos by custom departments which could lead to higher costs for importers and, in turn, reduce imports. However, the effectiveness of this new legislation will depend upon how strictly it is enforced. ### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 400

**Prices are not reflective of current market fundamentals** We still remain to be convinced that current prices are reflective of current market fundamentals. We work from the premise that at normal stock levels (65 days), fundamentally-driven prices (i.e. excluding non-fundamental influences) are fully justified at $4,400/t as opposed to $7700/t. We are also still of the opinion that the sheer weight of investment fund money flow into commodities that has created the current “multiplier effect” has been exaggerated by the lack of alternative investments (due to lower interest rates, poor profitability from within the non-cyclical equity markets etc). **Massive profits for speculators in 2009** There can be little doubt that market speculators made massive profits in commodities during 2009 looking at where prices finished the year in comparison with the very low levels that prevailed back in January (reflecting the backlash from the financial crisis). This year, it will be exceedingly difficult for hedge funds to repeat the level of profits seen in 2009 because commodity prices are very unlikely to repeat the magnitude of the increases that were seen in 2009 (136% for 3m copper). Also, as confidence returns to other markets there will be alternative investments competing with the commodities sector for investment money. There is also increasingly more cash being ploughed into the actively managed fund sector in comparison with the passive, long-only sector and substantially more money could be made out of shorting these markets (in order to rebase prices) than by adding further

length to existing levels (especially if one is of the view that certain of the base metal markets are profoundly over-priced relative to their fundamentals). **New tool for commodities may be launched** Another potential issue for commodities investors is the prospect of new financial regulations being introduced aimed at capping the level of hedge fund investment in these markets. One possible new alternative for the hedge funds may be Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) backed by physical LME warrantable base metals. Thus far, non-ferrous metal ETFs, which allow both institutional and retail investors to gain exposure to base metal prices by trading shares on stock exchanges, have been backed by futures contracts. However, potential changes to regulations surrounding investments in commodities may well make a product which is backed by a physical base metal more attractive. A number of banks are believed to be considering developing such a product modelled along the lines of the gold ETFs. These are backed by physical gold and have proved to be very popular over the past two years. Indeed, this may have prompted the recent acquisitions of major warehousing groups by both Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan. **Disconnect between future price forecasts and market fundamentals** Although speculative interest will continue to distort the relationship between market fundamentals and prices in the near to medium-term, we believe that the current magnitude of this disconnect is unsustainable (more so in the aluminium, nickel and zinc markets). And, while copper’s fundamentals remain relatively more robust in comparison with its base metal peers, given where copper prices are today in relation to stocks etc. the market does appear ripe for a downward price correction (and rebasing) despite the likelihood of a modest improvement in the fundamental picture moving forward. While we do not foresee a massive correction we would expect average prices in 2010 to fall below current quotes, to $7160/t ($3.25/lb) and to decline again in 2011 (-4.7%) to $6825/t ($3.10/lb) despite the moderate decline (3 days) in metal stocks from 71 days to 68 days. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - March 2010 Page 6 of 26 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments Much has been made of the impact of the investment community on commodity prices. In practice, it is not possible to fully quantify the level of fund activity in the metal markets, nor its impact upon price. However, that does not mean to say that looking at the trends in fund activity is not useful when considering future price moves in metals. Data indicate that the rally in prices that occurred in 2009 was simultaneous with rising fund interest in metals, implying a certain amount of causality from the latter to the former. The chart below shows an index put together using data from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, plotted against an index of the LME copper price. Under CFTC rules, traders engaging in index activi

ty in commodities (from index funds, swap dealers, pension funds, hedge funds and mutual funds) are required to file monthly reports with the CFTC, covering both direct investment through the futures markets, but also indirect investment via over-the-counter (OTC) swaps. Just to clarify, this only covers index-based investments, not actively managed positions. From these reports, data are published once a quarter that shows the notional value of index investments in specific markets, such as copper. It is to be expected that the notional value of index investments in copper would rise and fall with the copper price. However, the chart below shows that the degree of change in the value of copper investments is greater than that of the copper price. Effectively, the gap between the two lines since the end of 2008 represents the flow of additional funds into copper investments. ### **Index fund investment in copper rises faster than copper prices through 2009** Copper index fund investment

We believe there were two main reasons for this inflow. Firstly, during a period of economic recovery, industrial metals are an attractive option, being so leveraged to changes in the macro environment. The second factor was interest rates. As you can see from the chart below, headline interest rates in major economies reached very low levels at the start of 2009, particularly in the USA, coinciding with the start of the inflow of funds into commodities. The extremely low US interest rates enabled investors to borrow dollars for almost nothing, and invest them in assets, like base metals, with a greater yield – a process known as the dollar carry trade. Anecdotal accounts suggest this is still continuing, and we expect to see further inflows into commodity index investments when first quarter data are released. If interest rates were a decisive factor behind the inflow of money into metals over the past year, then likely they will be a key determinant of fund outflows – the reversal of the carry trade. With a slowing pace of economic recovery, the returns on metals are not likely to be anywhere near as high as they have been over the past year. And should interest rates begin to rise, the funding costs of the investments in metals will be higher. The turn in the interest rate cycle is thus a potential trigger for the unwinding of index investments in metals. When will headline interest rates start to rise once more? In some cases, they already have. India hiked both of its two policy interest rates during March. The move was overdue, and likely the first of many, given the high levels of inflation and strength of economic growth. In Brazil, inflationary pressures are also mounting, with the Brazilian Monetary Policy Committee statin

g during its March meeting that “all the information available shows deterioration of inflation dynamics”. We expect to see Brazilian rates increase in April. So too in China are inflationary concerns mounting, although here policy makers have a wider range of tools to tackle inflation than just interest rates. Further changes to bank lending and reserve requirements, as well as shifts in the exchange rate, are potential options. However, it is interest rates in the developed economies, particularly the USA, which are of primary concern, because it was the low borrowing cost of US dollars which facilitated investment in metals. Despite incredibly loose monetary policy and high fiscal spending, inflation in the USA is very low. The core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, was up by just 1.3% year on year in February. It is likely to remain at low levels for the next 12 months, given that consumer spending remains weak, unemployment high, and capacity utilisation rates extremely low. Thanks to such slack in the US economy, the Federal Open Market Committee has stated that it will keep rates at their current low “for an extended period”. We would not expect to see any rise in headline US interest rates before the November mid-term elections, and perhaps not until early 2011. In Europe, where the recovery is even more uncertain, interest rate rises are likely to lag any US moves. In short, an outflow of funds from commodity investments triggered by interest rate rises is not on the cards until the end of 2010. ### **US consumer price index – YoY % change** 6

Given that meaningful interest rates gains are not likely to occur anytime soon, the potential exists for the other main driver of fund inflows, the macro environment, to exert influence once more. Now the initial recovery phase is over, potential gains in metal prices are greatly diminished relative to last year. With stocks in aluminium, zinc and nickel extremely elevated, prices in these metals appear to be disconnected from the fundamentals. If so, shorting these metals becomes a much more attractive option for the actively-managed funds, which are able to reap large gains from driving prices down. The simple deterrent of negative returns from falling prices could be cause enough for index-b

ased investors to reassess the wisdom of allocating funds to metals, well before rising interest rates come into play. The global manufacturing purchasing manager’s index fell to 55.2 in February from 56.1 in January. Furthermore, the new orders to inventory ratio has fallen to its lowest level for ten months, implying that we have passed the peak of the boost to manufacturing activity caused by stimulus-induced restocking. Thus the pace of manufacturing expansion is expected to wane in the coming months. ### **Global manufacturing recovery has peaked** 65 1.4

**Global refined copper consumption to grow by 5.4% this year** We forecast that global refined copper consumption will increase by 5.4% this year to just above 18.2Mt. Previously we were forecasting growth of 5.7% to ~18.5Mt. The lower forecast reflected the knock–on effect of a downward revision we made to our Chinese estimate for last year. We lowered our 2009 Chinese demand estimate by ~150kt in line with a revised official number for Chinese refined production. In 2011 global demand is expected to grow more strongly, as the economies outside of China recover fully, which is reflected in our forecast of 6.6% growth to ~19.5Mt. **Chinese economic growth remains firm** Chinese economic growth remains incredibly robust despite some key economic indicators having moderated from the highs reached last year. Fixed Asset Investment (FAI) in the first two months of the year increased by 26.6% year on year. While this was down from the 35%+ growth recorded during mid2009, it was very much in line with the 27% average of the past five years. Also encouraging, in terms of future copper demand, was data which showed a 29.3% increase in floor space under construction during the first two months of the year from the corresponding period in 2009. Housing starts, meanwhile, rose by a stronger 37.5% year on year over the same two-month period. Growth within the construction sector is expected to remain strong through the year where copper demand will be supported by construction projects, which were started in 2009 and are now moving towards completion. Elsewhere demand will be supported by ongoing healthy growth in infrastructure investment and continued government fiscal stimulus measures. **No let up in Chinese d

emand** Reflecting the robust economy Chinese demand for copper remains healthy.  According to our sources order books for copper wire rod and copper and copper alloy products remained strong following the Chinese new year holiday.  Market conditions for magnet were particularly strong which resulted in some producers closing for only two days during the week-long holiday. 

**Strong growth in Chinese semis** Further underlining China’s robust demand was latest data from China’s Nonferrous Metal industry Association (CNIA) which showed a massive 31.1% jump in copper semis production during the first two months of 2010 from a year earlier.  However, apparent consumption increased by only 6.3% year on year during the two-month period, according to our calculations.  The difference between the two rates of growth reflected increased scrap usage and de-stocking by the copper semis producers.  This was not surprising in light of copper scrap imports increasing by 52.5% year on year through to February and the large build up of cathode through 2009.  Production of copper semis is expected to continue increasing, albeit not at such an emphatic rate.  However, refined consumption will not grow as strongly because of increased direct use of scrap and de-stocking.  This is reflected in our forecast of 9% growth in Chinese refined copper consumption this year to 7.1Mt.

**European manufacturing activity stalls** The recovery in European industrial activity has stalled already.  Activity in the euro zone unexpectedly contracted by 1.7% month-on-month in December, and remained down by 4.8% year on year. Worse still, in terms of copper demand, latest EU construction PM

**European copper semis production fell sharply in 2009** The extent of the downturn in Western European copper demand last year was highlighted recently by two of the region’s main producers of copper and copper alloy products reporting sharp falls in production.  KME, who has plants in Germany, Italy, France, Britain and Spain, reported that its output of copper and copper alloy products declined by 23.5% in 2009 to 437kt.  Elsewhere the German group, Wieland Werke, reported that its production of semi-finished copper products totalled 392kt during the 2008/2009 fiscal year that ended in September 2009.  This was down 24.8% (-129kt) from a year earlier.  These reductions were in line with the fall in Italian semis production last year. **Cathode demand remains weak** Unfortunately no significant recovery in European demand has occurred since the end of last year.  According to our sources cathode orders are reported to be down by 25% from levels witnessed two years ago.  A full sustainable recovery is expected to take time, especially in lieu of the fragile state of the regions’ construction sector. 

**French demand exceptionally weak** In France cathode demand is exceptionally weak following the closure of Nexans 300kt/a Chauny wire rod plant last year.  The company’s Lens plant may take up some of this lost production following the plant’s announcement that it is aiming to increase capacity from 165kt/a to 190-195kt/a by adding an extra shift. However, there have been problems with the casting furnace at the Lens plant because Nexans has preferred to increase the amount of scrap used rather than buy additional cathode.  According to our sources scrap material accounted for ~15% of the total furnace feed last year.  In addition to the problems associated with the furnace, the increased scrap intake will lower the quality of the rod produced.  Previously this would not have been a problem as the wire rod produced at the Lens plant was used to make energy cable which requires a lower grade of wire rod.  However, the Chauny plant produced a much higher grade of wire rod, as well as a greater variety, which will prove challenging for the Lens plant.  Therefore many are doubtful that the Lens plant will reach its production target of 190-195kt/a of copper wire rod this year.  With this in mind we forecast that French refined copper consumption will fall by 14% this year to 185kt.

From a relatively low base (e.g. assets such as Baluba, Chambishi and Muliashi in Zambia), the number of acquisitions and joint-venture initiatives has increased quite markedly of late and the more significant of these are listed below: 

- Aynak – Afghanistan (320kt/a Cu: Jiangxi Copper & CMGC) 

- Bahuerachi – Mexico (85kt/a Cu: Jinchuan) 

- Dikuluwe/Mashamba – DRC (400kt/a Cu: Sicomines) 

- Far South East – Philippines (150kt/a Cu: Zijin Mining) 

- Galeno – Peru (200kt/a Cu: MinMetals) 

- Mirador – Ecuador (60kt/a Cu: Tongling, CRCC) 

- Rio Blanco – Peru (160kt/a: Tongling & Zijin Mining) 

- Sierra Gorda – Chile (140kt/a Cu: State Grid) 

- Tampakan – Philippines (300kt/a Cu: Zijin Mining) 

- Toromocho – Peru (250kt/a Cu: Chinalco) 

In addition, Chinalco has stated that it would be interested in acquiring a stake in Oyu Tolgoi and China Sci-Tech is keen to purchase Chariot Resources which owns the Mina Justa project in Peru. 

**Oz Minerals looks to Mexico for new mine developments** Oz Minerals is looking to extend its operations base from Australia to Mexico having formed a joint venture with Azure Minerals to explore and develop the latter company’s 100%owned San Eduardo project.  Oz Minerals is to spend $3M over the next three years on exploration in order to earn a 51% stake in the project.  This interest could rise to 70% if the Australian company were to invest a further $10M.  San Eduardo adjoins Southern Copper’s El Tecolote polymetallic mine which closed in 1983. 

**Outotec to deliver roaster to Codelco – buys 100% of Ausmelt Ltd** Outotec has signed a contract with Codelco worth $156M to design and deliver a copper concentrate roasting plant, gas handling system and sulphuric acid plant for the Chilean company’s Mina Minera Minestro Hales project which is located close t

o the main Chuquicamata pit. Outotec’s turn-key plant delivery includes basic and detailed engineering, installation and start-up services. The Finnish company has also signed a Memorandum of Understanding to operate and maintain the plant for a period of two years following start up which is expected in early 2012. The Hales mine is scheduled to have its own dedicated concentrator and the requirement for the 550kt/a roaster (which will also produce 250kt/a of sulphuric acid) will be to reduce the arsenic content of the mine’s copper concentrates prior to smelting. Separately, Outotec announced that it had successfully acquired 100% of Australia’s Ausmelt Ltd. **UMMC to expand Pyshma** Urals Mining and Metals Co. expects to produce 356.9kt of refined copper from its Pyshma tankhouse in the Urals. This will represent an 8% increase over last year’s output of 330.1kt Cu. The company’s four smelters collectively despatched 276kt of blister to Pyshma, which is 5.7% less than in 2008 due to lower scrap availability and treatment at the Kirovgrad smelter. High-grade scrap consumption at Pyshma has remained virtually unchanged over the past two years at 53-55kt Cu (but still down from previous rates of 75-80kt/a). UMMC will invest $130M in upgrading the Pyshma refinery to raise output to 500kt/a Cu between 2012 and 2014 with over half of this budget to be spent during 2010. Meanwhile, UMMC’s neighbour, Russian Copper Company produced ~140kt at its two Russian refineries and SxEw mine last year and expects to raise this by 24% to 171kt in 2010.
